mainTopic: Why the משנה chose the field case for הפה שאסר הוא הפה שהתיר, and the dispute over whether someone who admits a debt and claims he repaid half must swear.
overview: The amud opens by finishing an earlier answer: between יהודה and גליל, the normal situation counts like a time of crisis. Then the גמרא asks why the משנה did not use other examples of הפה שאסר הוא הפה שהתיר. The loan case ('I borrowed and repaid') cannot work, because a loan made with witnesses can still be repaid without them. That means the משנה's contrast 'with witnesses he is not believed' would fail. The case 'your father had a מנה with me and I repaid half' cannot work either, because a ברייתא shows it is debated. The חכמים treat the man as a משיב אבידה who is exempt, while רבי אליעזר בן יעקב requires an oath. The גמרא asks why רבי אליעזר בן יעקב does not exempt a משיב אבידה. רב answers that a son was making a claim, but that answer runs into problems and is finally dropped. Instead, the גמרא says the dispute depends on רבה's reasoning for why a מודה מקצת must swear: a person does not dare deny a whole debt to his creditor's face. רבה's statement continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Judea and the Galilee count as a crisis situation
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes an earlier answer by explaining that the normal situation between יהודה and גליל is treated like a time of crisis.
steps.simpleTranslation: The usual situation between יהודה and גליל is considered like a time of crisis.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is wrapping up an answer from the previous discussion. It explains why a case involving people in יהודה and in גליל was described the way it was: travel between those two regions is normally treated like an emergency time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An emergency time (שעת חירום) can change how a case is judged. The גמרא says you do not need an actual war to have this status between יהודה and גליל, because the ordinary situation there is already like an emergency. This closes off the earlier question before the גמרא moves on.

keyTerms.meaning: the normal, usual situation
Judea and the Galilee, two separate regions of ארץ ישראל
a time of crisis or emergency (such as war)
they are similar to; they count as

steps.confusionAlert: This line is the end of an earlier discussion, not the start of a new topic. The new questions begin with the next line, וליתני.

phrases.english: That the usual situation of Judea and the Galilee
is like a time of crisis.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּסְתַם יְהוּדָה וּגְלִיל כִּשְׁעַת חֵירוּם דָּמוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer to a question asked just before this section.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the situation: the ordinary state of affairs counts as a crisis.
steps.terutzMaskana: Between יהודה and גליל, the normal situation is treated like a time of emergency.

steps.title: Why not use the case of a loan that was repaid?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה did not give the example of someone who says 'I borrowed a מנה from you and paid it back,' since he too should be believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה could have taught: רבי יהושע agrees that if someone tells his friend, 'I borrowed a מנה from you and I paid it back,' he is believed!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests another example the משנה could have used for רבי יהושע's rule. The borrower's own words are the only source for the loan, and those same words also say he repaid it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule of הפה שאסר הוא הפה שהתיר says that if the only reason we know about a problem is your own statement, we also believe the part of your statement that solves it. Here, nobody would know about the loan if the borrower had not told us, so his claim that he repaid it should be believed. The question is why the משנה chose the field case instead of this simpler one.

keyTerms.meaning: and let it teach (why didn't the משנה teach…?)
agrees, concedes
a sum of one hundred דינרים
I repaid it
believed, trusted

phrases.english: And let it teach: Rabbi Yehoshua agrees
in a case where one says to his fellow
"I borrowed a maneh from you
and I repaid it to you,"
that he is believed!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלִיתְנֵי: מוֹדֶה רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בְּאוֹמֵר לַחֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new question about the משנה's choice of example.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's choice of the field case to show רבי יהושע's principle.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A loan case seems to illustrate הפה שאסר הוא הפה שהתיר just as well, so why not use it?

steps.title: The loan case cannot support the ending of the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The משנה wanted to add an ending: 'if there are witnesses, he is not believed.' That ending does not work for a loan, because a loan made in front of witnesses can be repaid without witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the משנה wanted to teach in the later part: if there are witnesses that he borrowed and he says 'I repaid,' he is not believed. But we hold that someone who lends with witnesses does not need to be repaid with witnesses, so that ending would be wrong for a loan.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה needed a contrast in its second half: with witnesses, the person is not believed. That contrast works for the field case but not for a loan.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the field case, if witnesses say the field belonged to the father, the man's claim that he bought it is no longer protected, and he is not believed. In a loan case, even if witnesses saw the loan, the borrower is still believed when he says 'I paid,' because repayment does not need witnesses. So the loan case has no 'with witnesses he is not believed' half, and the משנה could not use it.

keyTerms.meaning: the later clause or ending of the משנה
witnesses
we hold, it is established for us
one who lends

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying the borrower is disbelieved. It is saying the opposite: he is believed even with witnesses. That is exactly why the loan case cannot show a contrast between 'no witnesses' and 'witnesses.'
steps.whyThisMatters: The rule that a loan made with witnesses does not need witnesses for repayment is a basic principle in monetary law, and it explains why loan cases behave differently from ownership cases.

phrases.english: Because it wants
to teach in the later clause:
If there are witnesses
that he borrowed from him,
and he says: I repaid it —
he is not believed,
phrases.notes: This is the ending the משנה would have needed if it used a loan case. The next line shows why that ending would be wrong.

phrases.english: but don't we hold
one who lends to his fellow with witnesses —
does not need to repay him with witnesses.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Structural: the case the משנה chose had to fit both halves of the משנה.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A loan case would work just as well as the field case.
steps.terutzMaskana: A loan case cannot produce the 'with witnesses, not believed' ending, because repayment does not need witnesses.

steps.title: Why not use the case of 'I repaid your father half'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests another example: someone tells the son, 'your father had a מנה with me, and I repaid him half.' He too should be believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה could have taught: רבי יהושע agrees that if someone tells his friend, 'Your father has a מנה with me, and I paid him half,' he is believed!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests a second alternative example of הפה שאסר. The son knew nothing about the debt, and the man who admits it also says that half was already paid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This case also has no witnesses, and it is not about a loan the son himself made. Since the debt is known only from this man's words, the half-payment claim should be believed. So the גמרא asks why the משנה did not use this case.

keyTerms.meaning: in my hand; I am holding it (I owe it)
half
literally 'I fed him'; here, I paid him

phrases.english: And let it teach: Rabbi Yehoshua agrees
in a case where one says to his fellow:
Your father has a maneh in my hand,
and I gave him half —
phrases.notes: Literally "I fed him half." It means he already paid back half of the debt.

phrases.english: that he is believed!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלִיתְנֵי: מוֹדֶה רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בְּאוֹמֵר לַחֲבֵירוֹ: מָנֶה לְאָבִיךְ בְּיָדִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the loan case was rejected, the גמרא proposes a different alternative example.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's choice of the field case.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: This half-repaid case seems to show הפה שאסר הוא הפה שהתיר, so why was it not used?

steps.title: That case is a debate among the תנאים, and neither view fits
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the half-repaid case is debated. According to the רבנן he counts as someone returning a lost object, and according to רבי אליעזר בן יעקב he must take an oath. Either way, it does not fit the משנה's simple 'he is believed.'
steps.simpleTranslation: According to whom would the משנה teach this? If according to the רבנן, they said he counts as one who returns a lost object. If according to רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, he said an oath is needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that this case would not fit the משנה. Each side of a תנאים debate treats it differently from a simple case of being believed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן treat him as a משיב אבידה, someone who honestly returns what the son did not know about, so the case already has its own ruling with a different reason. רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says he must swear an oath, so he is not simply 'believed' the way the משנה puts it. Since neither opinion matches the משנה's model, the משנה used the field case instead.

keyTerms.meaning: according to whom?
the Sages (the majority view)
one who returns a lost object
a תנא who disagrees with the רבנן here
an oath

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה chose the field case because the alternatives do not fit. In the loan case, the borrower is believed even with witnesses, so there is no contrast. The half-repaid case is debated, and neither side gives a plain 'he is believed.'

phrases.english: According to whom?
If according to the Rabbis —
didn't they say
he is one who returns a lost object.

phrases.aramaic: אִי אַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב —
phrases.english: If according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov —
didn't he say an oath is required.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing that the suggested case is debated and fits neither opinion.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The half-repaid case is a plain example of being believed through הפה שאסר.
steps.terutzMaskana: For the רבנן it falls under משיב אבידה. For רבי אליעזר בן יעקב it needs an oath. Neither fits the משנה's wording.

steps.title: The ברייתא behind the half-repaid debate
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא where רבי אליעזר בן יעקב requires an oath in the half-repaid case, and the חכמים exempt him as a משיב אבידה.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says: Sometimes a person swears because of his own claim. How so? 'Your father had a מנה with me and I paid him half.' He must swear, and this is someone who swears because of his own claim. The חכמים say: He is just like someone returning a lost object, and he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the source for what it said in step 5. This ברייתא shows the half-repaid case really is debated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nobody sued this man. He admitted the debt himself. רבי אליעזר בן יעקב still makes him swear about the half he says he paid. The חכמים say that since he told the truth on his own, he is like someone returning a lost object, so we trust him without an oath.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is taught (in a ברייתא)
Swears because of his own claim, when no one else claimed anything
A sum of one hundred זוז
Half
Someone returning a lost object, who is trusted without an oath

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: As it is taught: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says:
There are times when a person swears
because of his own claim.
How so? 'Your father had a maneh with me,
and I gave him half.'
He must swear,
and this is one who swears because of his own claim.
And the Sages say:
He is only like one who returns a lost object, and he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the debate mentioned in step 5
steps.raayaObject: That the half-repaid case is debated between the רבנן and רבי אליעזר בן יעקב
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of רבי אליעזר בן יעקב and the חכמים

steps.title: Does רבי אליעזר בן יעקב reject the rule of returning a lost object?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי אליעזר בן יעקב does not exempt this man as a משיב אבידה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does רבי אליעזר בן יעקב not hold that someone returning a lost object is exempt?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי אליעזר בן יעקב. The man admitted on his own, so why should he need to swear?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Exempting a משיב אבידה from an oath is an accepted rule. It seems strange that רבי אליעזר בן יעקב would reject it. So the גמרא wants to know why he treats this man differently.

keyTerms.meaning: He does not hold of
Exempt

phrases.english: And Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov,
does he not hold that one who returns a lost object is exempt?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב לֵית לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the opinion of רבי אליעזר בן יעקב in the ברייתא
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב's requirement of an oath
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The man admitted on his own, so he should be exempt like any משיב אבידה

steps.title: רב: a minor was making a claim against him
steps.stepSummary: רב explains that in this case a קטן was claiming against him, so he is not simply volunteering.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: The case is where a minor makes a claim against him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers the question. Someone did claim against the man, so he is not like a person returning a lost object.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A משיב אבידה is exempt because nobody pushed him to admit anything. Here the son claimed against him first. So his admission came in response to a claim, and רבי אליעזר בן יעקב requires an oath.

keyTerms.meaning: When someone makes a claim against him
A minor

phrases.english: Rav said: It is where a minor makes a claim against him.
phrases.notes: The minor is the lender's son. He claims that none of his father's loan was paid back.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: The man admitted completely on his own
steps.terutzMaskana: The son claimed first, so the man is not a משיב אבידה

steps.title: But we do not swear on a minor's claim
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that a minor's claim cannot create an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the Master said: We do not swear on the claim of a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, or a minor!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב's answer using a known rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קטן's claim has no legal weight to force an oath. So if the claimant is a minor, it is as if nobody claimed. Then the man is again like a משיב אבידה, and the original question returns.

keyTerms.meaning: But the Master said
A deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, and a minor

phrases.english: But didn't the Master say:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין נִשְׁבָּעִין עַל טַעֲנַת חֵרֵשׁ שׁוֹטֶה וְקָטָן!
phrases.english: We do not swear on the claim of a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, or a minor!

steps.kashyaTarget: רב's explanation that a קטן made the claim
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A minor's claim cannot force an oath, so it cannot explain why the man must swear

steps.title: The 'minor' is really an adult
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that רב meant an adult, called a 'minor' because he knows little about his father's affairs.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'minor' mean? An adult. Why does he call him a minor? Because when it comes to his father's matters, he is like a minor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא saves רב's answer by reading the word 'minor' differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The son is an adult, so his claim has full legal weight and can force an oath. רב called him a 'minor' only because he does not really know his father's business. That keeps both parts of the answer working.

keyTerms.meaning: An adult
He calls him
His father's matters

phrases.english: What is 'minor'? An adult.
And why does he call him a minor?
Because regarding his father's matters, he is like a minor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 9 by reinterpreting רב's word
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Minor' means a real minor, whose claim cannot force an oath
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Minor' means an adult who does not know his father's affairs, so his claim is valid
steps.confusionAlert: The son is not actually a child. 'קטן' here is just a way of saying he knows as little about his father's affairs as a child would.

steps.title: Then it is not 'his own claim'
steps.stepSummary: If the son made the claim, why does the ברייתא call it swearing 'on his own claim'?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why is it called 'his own claim'? It is someone else's claim!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now challenges the wording of the ברייתא based on the new explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once we say that an adult son claimed against the man, the oath comes from the son's claim. That does not fit the ברייתא's words 'swears on his own claim.'

keyTerms.meaning: If so
The claim of other people

phrases.english: If so, 'his own claim'?
It is the claim of others!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ברייתא's wording in light of step 10
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If an adult son claimed, the oath comes from his claim, not from the man's own claim

steps.title: Someone else's claim, but his own admission
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the claim came from the son, but the oath comes from the man's own partial admission.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is the claim of others, and his own admission.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what 'his own' means in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The son made the claim. But the oath happens because the man himself admitted part of the debt. So 'his own' refers to his admission, not to the claim.

keyTerms.meaning: His own admission

phrases.english: The claim of others, and his own admission.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'His own claim' means nobody else claimed
steps.terutzMaskana: 'His own' refers to his own admission, which causes the oath

steps.title: That is true of every oath case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that every oath case has someone else's claim and the person's own admission, so this case is nothing special.
steps.simpleTranslation: All claims are cases of someone else's claim and his own admission!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the last answer. This challenge knocks out רב's whole way of explaining the ברייתא, and the next step gives a new explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every partial-admission oath comes from someone else's claim plus the person's own admission. So that cannot be what רבי אליעזר בן יעקב meant by 'פעמים,' which suggests an unusual case. The next step answers this with a new approach.

keyTerms.meaning: All the claims
They are

phrases.english: All claims,
are the claim of others and one's own admission!

steps.triggerLanguage: כּוּלְּהִי טַעֲנָתָא, טַעֲנַת אֲחֵרִים וְהוֹדָאַת עַצְמוֹ נִינְהוּ
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That describes every oath case, but the ברייתא's 'פעמים' implies a special case

steps.title: A new explanation: the dispute is about רבה's principle
steps.stepSummary: After rejecting the earlier explanation, the גמרא proposes that רבי אליעזר בן יעקב and the חכמים disagree about רבה's principle.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, here they disagree about the teaching of רבה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops its earlier answer and offers a fresh explanation of the dispute. This line sets up the next move, which quotes רבה's principle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 13 showed that "someone else's claim plus his own admission" is true of every oath, so רב's idea of a son making a claim is dropped. The new idea is that the argument turns on why the Torah demands an oath from a מודה מקצת in the first place, and that reason is רבה's teaching, which comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. It signals that the earlier answer is dropped and a new one is coming.
They disagree.
An אמורא whose reasoning about partial admission is quoted next.

phrases.english: Rather, here
phrases.notes: "Here" means the dispute between רבי אליעזר בן יעקב and the חכמים in the ברייתא.

phrases.english: they disagree about the teaching of רבה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 13 knocks down רב's approach (steps 8–12, a son making a claim), the גמרא gives a new answer to step 7's question of why רבי אליעזר בן יעקב requires an oath.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframes the basis of the dispute
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's phrase 'on his own claim' was explained by the man's own partial admission, but that is true of every oath.
steps.terutzMaskana: The תנאים disagree about how far רבה's reason for the oath of a מודה מקצת reaches.

steps.title: רבה: why a partial admitter must swear
steps.stepSummary: רבה begins explaining why a מודה מקצת must swear. There is a חזקה that a borrower would not boldly deny the whole debt to his creditor's face. So the fact that he did not deny everything does not prove he is honest, because he may have held back only out of embarrassment. רבה's statement continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבה said: Why did the Torah say that one who admits part of the claim must swear? Because of a חזקה that a person does not act brazenly in front of his creditor. This borrower really wanted to deny the whole debt. The reason he did not deny all of it is that a person does not act so brazenly.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes רבה's reason for the oath of a מודה מקצת. This is the principle the תנאים are said to disagree about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think: he could have denied the whole debt, so why not believe him about the rest? רבה answers that a person does not dare deny everything to his creditor's face. So his holding back proves nothing, and his denial of the rest is not automatically trusted. רבה's statement, and its use to explain the dispute in the ברייתא, continue on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: One who admits part of the claim against him and denies the rest.
A presumption about how people usually behave.
Acts brazenly, literally 'makes his face bold'.
His creditor, the person he owes money to.
To deny it, meaning to deny the debt.

steps.whatToRemember: רבה: a מודה מקצת may really want to deny the whole debt but does not dare to lie to his creditor's face. So his partial admission does not earn him trust about the rest. This is the base for the dispute between רבי אליעזר בן יעקב and the חכמים.
steps.confusionAlert: It is easy to assume that a partial admission makes the borrower look honest. רבה says the opposite: it makes him look like someone who would have denied everything if he had the nerve.
steps.whyThisMatters: רבה's חזקה is the basic reason given for the oath of a מודה מקצת. Here it becomes the key to the dispute between רבי אליעזר בן יעקב and the חכמים.

phrases.english: As רבה said:
Why did the Torah say
that one who admits part of the claim must swear?
It is a presumption that a person does not act brazenly
in front of his creditor.
And this borrower wanted to deny all of it,
and the reason he did not deny it all to him

phrases.aramaic: מִשּׁוּם דְּאֵין אָדָם מֵעִיז פָּנָיו הוּא.
phrases.english: is because a person does not act brazenly.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַבָּה: מִפְּנֵי מָה אָמְרָה תּוֹרָה מוֹדֶה מִקְצָת הַטַּעֲנָה יִשָּׁבַע

steps.mimraCoreRuling: A מודה מקצת is not trusted just because he could have denied everything, since a person will not boldly deny a whole debt to his creditor. He may have wanted to deny everything.
